title: Aligning Language Models with Selective Prediction
claim: Perfect calibration doesn't guarantee good selective prediction ordering; aligning directly to the selective-prediction objective beats competing methods on risk metrics.
layout: 2 panels: stacked ECE vs AURC schematics left, grouped bar chart right
description: The left half has two stacked schematics separated by a dashed line. The top one is titled 'Perfect Calibration (Metric: ECE)'. It shows an arrow running from high to low confidence, with three rounded boxes labelled 0.8, 0.6 and 0.4. Each box holds circles marked with a check or a cross. The correct and incorrect predictions are mixed across the boxes, and magenta curved arrows with an X flag that this violates perfect selective-prediction ordering. A dotted threshold line splits 'answer' from 'abstain'. The bottom schematic is titled 'Perfect Selective Prediction (Metric: AURC)'. There, all checks sit above the threshold and all crosses sit below it. The right half is a grouped bar chart of AURC and Risk@10, @25 and @50 for BASE, RLVR, RLCR and RLSR (Ours). The orange RLSR bars are outlined in black and starred, and they are the lowest in each group. A 'Lower is better' note sits in the legend.
caption: (Left) Perfect confidence calibration does not translate to perfect selective prediction, and vice versa; (Right) Our RLSR aligns LLMs with selective prediction (SP) and substantially improves upon competing methods in terms of SP metrics: AURC and Risk@ k.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as critical decision-making components in high-stakes real-world AI systems, rendering LLM reliability a foremost practical concern. In this paper, we focus on enhancing LLM reliability through selective prediction (SP), a strategy that allows an LLM to only predict for inputs where it is likely to be correct (i.e., coverage) and hence reduce the error rate (i.e., risk) on that portion of inputs---flagging the remaining inputs for future human discretion. In other words, SP improves LLM reliability by balancing the risk-coverage trade-off and enabling seamless human-AI collaboration. To integrate SP into LLMs, we focus on the LLM post-training alignment stage and propose to align LLMs with SP performance metrics, in contrast with existing LLM alignment methods that focus primarily on correctness or calibration metrics. Specifically, we propose a novel alignment framework, Reinforcement Learning for Selection Reward (RLSR), which targets the area under the risk-coverage curve (AURC)---a popular SP performance metric---as its alignment objective. RLSR achieves substantially better risk-coverage trade-off compared to multiple alignment baselines on both in-domain and out-of-domain tasks.
